title: Back from the edge
hook: Your company is losing hundreds of millions of dollars, and its fans are leaving. Can you save it?

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Apple is for what comes next

intro.text: Late 1996. You are running Apple, the maker of the Mac, and it has just lost $816 million in a single year. Mac sales keep falling, and the board wants a plan before buyers give up on the Mac for good.

d1.title: The missing software
d1.setup: The heart of the problem is the Mac's operating system, the main program that runs the computer. It is old, and Apple's own new one, Copland, was years late, and Apple has put it on hold. Be, a young company, has fast new software that is still being tested. NeXT, the company Apple's co-founder started in 1985, has software that is older but proven.
d1.question: Where do you get the Mac's new software?
d1.advisor: Whatever we choose, we are betting the company on it. And every month we wait, more buyers move to Windows.

options.label: Restart Copland and give your team about 18 more months. You keep control, but you lose time.
options.outcome: Your engineers get their 18 months. But the deadlines keep slipping, and every month the Mac falls further behind Windows.
options.why: Copland had already slipped for years. Giving a late project more time left Apple with nothing new to sell.
options.better: Buy software that already works, even if it is not perfect, and build the next Mac on it.
options.takeaway: In 1996 you gave a late project more time instead of buying something that already worked.

options.label: Buy NeXT for $400 million. It costs the most, but its software already works.
options.outcome: On 20 December 1996 you agree to buy NeXT for $400 million. Its software will become the heart of the next Mac system, and Apple's co-founder, who started NeXT, comes back to Apple as an adviser.
options.why: You bought software that already worked, along with the people who knew how to use it, including the man who started Apple.
options.takeaway: In 1996 you bought working software and the people behind it.

options.label: Buy Be for about $300 million. Its software is fast and modern, but still being tested.
options.outcome: You buy Be. Its software is quick, but it needs years more work before it can run every Mac, and the Mac keeps falling behind while you wait.
options.why: Be's software was exciting, but unfinished. You paid for a promise when Apple needed something it could ship.
options.better: Choose the software that is already finished and tested, even if it costs more.
options.takeaway: In 1996 you paid for fast software that wasn't ready.

text.text: July 1997. Apple is still losing money, and the CEO who signed the NeXT deal resigns after 18 months. The returning co-founder's role grows fast, and from here on, you play him: the calls are now yours.
July 1997. Copland is still not ready, Apple is still losing money, and the board is losing patience. You keep your job, but only just.
July 1997. Be's software is still not ready for the Mac, Apple is still losing money, and the board is losing patience. You keep your job, but only just.

d2.title: Deal with the rival?
d2.setup: For years Apple has fought Microsoft in court over how the Mac looks. Yet Microsoft also makes Office for the Mac, and many buyers would leave if it stopped. Now Microsoft offers to end the fight and put $150 million into Apple.
d2.question: What do you do about Microsoft?
d2.advisor: Our fans see Microsoft as the enemy. But they also use its Office on their Macs every day.

options.label: Keep fighting in court. A win could make Microsoft pay, and your fans stay loyal.
options.outcome: The court fight drags on. Microsoft goes quiet about new Office versions for the Mac, and schools and offices start asking if the Mac has a future.
options.why: Pride won the day, but the Mac needed Office far more than Apple needed to win in court.
options.better: End the fight, take the money, and lock in Office for the Mac.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you kept fighting a rival whose software your buyers needed.

options.label: Raise money by selling shares or borrowing, and stay free of your biggest rival.
options.outcome: You raise the money, but it costs a lot, because lenders can see the losses. The fight with Microsoft goes on, and so do the doubts about Office.
options.why: You found cash, but at a high price, and the bigger risk, losing Office, was still there.
options.better: Take the deal that brings both money and a promise of Office.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you paid a high price for money and left the Office risk open.

options.label: Take the deal. You get money and Office for years, but your fans may feel betrayed.

outcome.text: On 6 August 1997 at Macworld Boston, you announce the deal. Microsoft buys $150 million of Apple shares, the long court fight ends, and Office keeps coming to the Mac. Part of the crowd boos, but Apple's share price jumps 35% that day.
You sign the deal. Microsoft buys $150 million of Apple shares, the long court fight ends, and Office keeps coming to the Mac. Some fans are angry, but investors are relieved.

options.why: You put the Mac's future ahead of an old fight. The money helped, but the promise of Office mattered even more.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you made peace with a rival to keep your customers' key software.

d3.title: Too many products

setup.text: September 1997. The board makes you interim CEO. You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer called the Newton, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

Money is tighter than ever. You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

The new money will not last long. You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

d3.question: What do you do with all these products?
d3.advisor: Even shop staff can't explain which Mac to buy. But every product we cut has buyers, and people who build it.

options.label: Cut to four Macs, home and pro, desktop and laptop, and end the clones. Thousands lose jobs.

outcome.text: You cut more than 70% of the products, down to a grid of four boxes. Apple stops licensing the Mac and buys the main Mac business of Power Computing, a clone maker. More than 3,000 jobs go, and early in 1998 the Newton goes too.
You cut the list down to four Macs and end the clone deals. It is painful, and thousands of jobs go, but costs fall fast and buyers can finally understand what Apple sells.

options.why: You stopped spending on things that didn't sell and put all your effort into a few products people could understand.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you cut to a few products and did them well.

options.label: Keep every product and add more clone makers. More Macs in use could bring more fans.
options.outcome: Sales hold up for a while, but every clone sold is a Mac that Apple didn't sell, and the losses keep growing.
options.why: The clones paid Apple only $80 a machine, and the long product list kept wasting money.
options.better: Cut to a few products people can understand, and stop the clones.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you kept everything and let the clones eat your sales.

options.label: Cut a few weak products, but keep the clones and the fees they pay.
options.outcome: The list gets a little shorter, but buyers are still confused, and the clone makers keep taking your best customers.
options.why: A small trim felt safe, but it fixed neither the confusing list nor the clones.
options.better: Make the deep cut: a few clear products, and no more clones.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you trimmed when Apple needed a deep cut.

d4.title: What does Apple stand for?

setup.text: With so many products, even your own people can't say what Apple is about, and buyers have heard two years of bad news. Money is tight, but the agency behind Apple's famous 1984 ad is ready to work with you again.
Buyers have heard two years of bad news about Apple, and money is tight. But the agency behind Apple's famous 1984 ad is ready to work with you again.

d4.question: How do you talk to buyers now?
d4.advisor: Ads won't fix a bad product. But if people stop believing in Apple, even a good product won't sell.

options.label: Run ads about what Apple stands for. They cost a lot and don't sell any one Mac.

outcome.text: On 28 September 1997, your "Think different" ads appear on US TV, during the first network showing of the film Toy Story. They come from the same agency as the 1984 ad, and they talk about Apple's values, not its chips.
Your new ads talk about the people who use a Mac, not about chips. Slowly, the talk about Apple changes from whether it will survive to what it will do next.

options.why: You reminded people why they loved Apple, at the moment they had stopped believing in it.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you sold what Apple stood for, not its speed.

options.label: Run ads showing that a Mac beats a Windows PC on speed and price.
options.outcome: The ads make their case, but buyers have heard speed claims from everyone. Apple starts to sound like one more PC maker.
options.why: Comparing chips was a fight on Windows' ground, and it didn't fix Apple's damaged name.
options.better: Remind people what Apple stands for, then give them a product that proves it.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you sold specs when Apple needed belief.

options.label: Stop almost all advertising, and save the cash for the products.
options.outcome: You save money, but Apple goes quiet just when people are asking whether it will survive, and shops push buyers toward Windows PCs.
options.why: Going silent looked like giving up. A brand in trouble needs to speak up, not disappear.
options.better: Spend on one clear message about what Apple stands for.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you went silent when Apple most needed to be heard.

text.text: In October 1997 Apple reports a loss of $1 billion for the year, much of it one-time costs for the clean-up. But the cuts start working, and in the three months to December, Apple makes a profit of $47 million. The home desktop box in your grid still has no product.
The cuts hurt, but costs fall fast and the losses begin to shrink. The home desktop box in your grid still has no product.
1998. You still sell dozens of products, and the losses keep coming. Apple needs one computer that people actually want.
1998. Apple is a little smaller and the losses are shrinking, but it still has nothing that excites home buyers.

d5.title: A computer for everyone
d5.setup: Apple needs a desktop for homes and schools, one that brings in new buyers, not just old fans. At the same time, more and more people want a computer for one reason: to get on the internet.
d5.question: What kind of home computer do you build?
d5.advisor: Plain and cheap is safe, because buyers know what they are getting. Something new could be a big hit, or a very public flop.

options.label: Make a cheap, plain Mac that looks like any PC. It feels safe, but it is easy to ignore.
options.outcome: It sells a little, mostly to Mac fans. In a shop full of beige boxes, nobody else notices it.
options.why: Copying the PC makers gave buyers no reason to switch to a Mac.
options.better: Build something new and simple that first-time buyers will want to own.
options.takeaway: In 1998 you built a safe computer that nobody noticed.

options.label: Build a bright, see-through, all-in-one Mac for the internet, with no floppy drive.

outcome.text: On 6 May 1998 you show the iMac, at $1,299. It has a see-through case, it is built for the internet, and it has no floppy drive. It reaches shops on 15 August and many sell out. In six weeks you sell 278,000, and almost 3 in 10 early buyers have never owned a computer.
Your bright, simple Mac is a surprise hit with first-time buyers, although some old fans miss the floppy drive.

options.why: You built something new for people who had never owned a computer, and made the internet easy for them.
options.takeaway: In 1998 you built a new kind of computer for first-time buyers.

options.label: Skip home buyers. Serve the designers and schools who already love the Mac.
options.outcome: Your loyal users stay, but they are a shrinking group, and the big wave of new home buyers goes to Windows.
options.why: Old fans alone could not pay for Apple's future. The growth was with new buyers.
options.better: Build a computer that brings in people who have never owned a Mac.
options.takeaway: In 1998 you served your fans and missed the new buyers.

text.text: In the year to September 1998, Apple makes a profit of $309 million, its first profitable year since 1995, and its cash grows to $2.3 billion. In the last three months of 1998 it sells 519,000 iMacs, and makes a profit for the fifth quarter in a row.
You fixed the software, focused the products and gave buyers a reason to believe again. Apple is making money and has a clear future.
Apple survives, but it is stuck with old software it never managed to replace. It makes a little money, yet buyers and software makers see the Mac as a side choice, not the future.
Apple survives, but Be's software takes years to finish, and the Mac stays behind. It makes a little money, yet buyers see it as a side choice, not the future.
Apple survives, but it stays small and stuck. It makes a little money, yet buyers and software makers see it as a side choice, not the future.

collapse.title: The lights go out
collapse.text: The losses never stop, and the cash runs out. Apple is sold off in pieces, and the Mac becomes a memory.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: The board has seen enough. After three costly calls, it asks someone else to save Apple.

realHistory: Apple lost $816 million in 1996 and $1 billion in 1997. In December 1996 it bought NeXT for $400 million, and its co-founder came back, becoming interim CEO in September 1997. In 1997 Microsoft bought $150 million of Apple shares and their court fight ended. Apple cut more than 70% of its products, ended the Mac clones and launched the "Think different" ads. The iMac came out in 1998. In the year to September 1998 Apple made $309 million, its first profitable year since 1995.
